units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive there. For each $z\in\mathbb R$, define the
exact multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=\begin{cases}e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)},&\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta,\\0,&\boldsymbol\xi\notin D_\delta,\end{cases}$$
and define the paraxial multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}.$$
The exact scalar and paraxial scalar propagators are the $L^2$ equivalence
classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
For complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ at frequency
$\omega$, the real-field encoding assigns the maps
$\mathbf E,\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by
$$\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf e e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right),\qquad \mathbf B(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf b e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right).$$
In the SI field interpretation, $\mathbf e$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$
and $\mathbf b$ has units tesla. The candidate is an **exact
source-free vacuum plane-wave mode** precisely when these real fields are
jointly $C^1$ and satisfy, pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$,
$$\operatorname{div}\mathbf E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf B=c^{-2}\partial_t\mathbf E,$$
the zero-source specialization of the adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell branch.
The longitudinal electric coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. For $n\ge1$, these are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of The derivative and the Riemann integral of a vector-valued function: an intrinsic derivative and a componentwise integral.

For $n=0$, use the zero-space case directly, without invoking that supplier's positive-codomain standing hypothesis. The space $\mathbb R^0$ has only its zero vector and carries the zero Euclidean norm and its induced metric (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5, The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms). Whenever the line map is defined near $0$, every difference quotient for real $t\ne0$ is this zero vector; define $D_vf(a)=0$. This is the unique possible derivative value, and its normwise difference-quotient error is exactly zero for all such $t$, so the real parameter still approaches an actual limit point. Every existing coordinate direction therefore has $\partial_jf(a)=0$; these zero-valued partial maps are continuous in the induced norm metrics. If the source dimension is zero, there are no partial indices and the sole direction is $v=0$; its constant line map is defined near $0$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: For $r>0$, [F4] identifies the angular vector field $-y\partial_x+x\partial_y$ with $\partial_\phi$. By [F2]–[F3], differentiating the integer winding factor gives $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z=-i\partial_\phi(fe^{i\ell\phi}) =\ell fe^{i\ell\phi}=\ell u_z$. The required axis form makes $u_z$ smooth at the origin: for $\ell\ge0$ its angular factor is $(x+iy)^\ell$, and for $\ell<0$ it is $(x-iy)^{|\ell|}$, each multiplied by the smooth radial factor $g(x^2+y^2)$. The rotation vector field vanishes at the origin, so the same identity holds there as well.

Step 1.1 gives $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z=\ell u_z$ everywhere, hence $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z\in L^2$ because $u_z\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. Therefore $\langle L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z,u_z\rangle_2 =\int_{\mathbb R^2}\ell|u_z|^2\,d^2x =\ell\langle u_z,u_z\rangle_2$; the denominator is positive since $u_z$ is nonzero. Division proves the claimed identity.

of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Fix a named positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$, spatial domain $\mathbb R^3$, and time domain $\mathbb R$. Adopt SI
units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive there. For each $z\in\mathbb R$, define the
exact multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=\begin{cases}e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)},&\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta,\\0,&\boldsymbol\xi\notin D_\delta,\end{cases}$$
and define the paraxial multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}.$$
The exact scalar and paraxial scalar propagators are the $L^2$ equivalence
classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
For complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ at frequency
$\omega$, the real-field encoding assigns the maps
$\mathbf E,\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by
$$\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf e e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right),\qquad \mathbf B(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf b e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right).$$
In the SI field interpretation, $\mathbf e$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$
and $\mathbf b$ has units tesla. The candidate is an **exact
source-free vacuum plane-wave mode** precisely when these real fields are
jointly $C^1$ and satisfy, pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$,
$$\operatorname{div}\mathbf E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf B=c^{-2}\partial_t\mathbf E,$$
the zero-source specialization of the adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell branch.
The longitudinal electric coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

Let $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, and $s\in[0,\delta^2]$. Define

$$R(s):=1-\frac{s}{2}-\sqrt{1-s}.$$

Then

$$R(s)=\frac{s^2}{4\left(1-\frac{s}{2}+\sqrt{1-s}\right)},\qquad 0\le R(s)\le\frac{s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},$$

and

$$\left|e^{izk_0\sqrt{1-s}}-e^{izk_0(1-s/2)}\right| \le \frac{|z|k_0s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}.$$

More generally, for all real $a,b$,
$$|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|.$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, and $z\in\mathbb R$. For every
$u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ whose Fourier transform is supported, up
to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$,

$$\left\|u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z)-u_{\mathrm{par}}(z)\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)} \le \frac{|z|k_0\delta^4}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}\left\|u_0\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)},$$

where the propagated fields are exactly those of the angular-spectrum
Definition. For a source-free monochromatic vacuum plane-wave mode with
$\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$, $|\mathbf q|\le\delta k_0$,
$k_z:=\sqrt{k_0^2-|\mathbf q|^2}$, and complex electric amplitude
$\mathbf e=(\mathbf e_\perp,e_z)$, use the complex-bilinear convention
$\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf e_\perp:=q_xe_x+q_ye_y$ with no conjugation,

$$e_z=-\frac{\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf e_\perp}{k_z},\qquad |e_z|\le\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{1-\delta^2}}|\mathbf e_\perp|.$$

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim: Set $\delta_n:=1/(n+2)$ and $R_n:=\delta_n k_0/(2\pi)$. Let $\Xi_n:=[R_n(1-\delta_n/4),R_n(1-\delta_n/8)] \times[0,R_n\delta_n/8]$. Its side lengths are both $R_n\delta_n/8>0$, so [F4] gives $0<|\Xi_n|=R_n^2\delta_n^2/64<\infty$. Define $\widehat u_{0,n}:=A_\star|\Xi_n|^{-1/2}\mathbf 1_{\Xi_n}$; then $\|\widehat u_{0,n}\|_2=A_\star$. For $\mathbf q=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ with $\boldsymbol\xi\in\Xi_n$, $q_x\ge\delta_n k_0(1-\delta_n/4)>\delta_n k_0(1-\delta_n)$ and $|\mathbf q|^2\le\delta_n^2k_0^2[(1-\delta_n/8)^2+(\delta_n/8)^2] \le\delta_n^2k_0^2$; hence this nonzero spectrum lies in the angular cone and concentrates near its outer radius.

Let $u_{0,n}:=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\widehat u_{0,n}$ and $z_n:=8\pi/(k_0\delta_n^4)>0$. This fixes the scale in [F6] at $8\pi$. By [F3], $\|u_{0,n}\|_2=A_\star$, so each input is nonzero and admissible for the refuted statement.

For $\boldsymbol\xi\in\Xi_n$, put $s_n:=|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/k_0^2$. Step 1.1 gives $(1-\delta_n/4)^2\le s_n/\delta_n^2\le1$, so this ratio tends to $1$ uniformly on $\Xi_n$. Also $0\le s_n\le\delta_n^2$, and $|1-\sqrt{1-s_n}|=s_n/(1+\sqrt{1-s_n})\le s_n$, so $1-s_n/2+\sqrt{1-s_n}\to2$ uniformly. By [F2], the relative phase difference is $\Delta_n:=z_nk_0R(s_n) =2\pi(s_n/\delta_n^2)^2/(1-s_n/2+\sqrt{1-s_n})$, which tends uniformly to $\pi$.

The actual exact-minus-paraxial phase is $-\Delta_n$, so [F5] makes the modulus of the multiplier difference $|e^{i\Delta_n}-1|$. Put $u=e^{i\Delta_n}-1$ and $v=e^{i\pi}-1$. By [F7], $\bigl||u|-|v|\bigr|\le|u-v|$; [F5] gives $|v|=2$, and [F2] gives $|u-v|=|e^{i\Delta_n}-e^{i\pi}|\le|\Delta_n-\pi|\to0$ uniformly on $\Xi_n$. Thus the multiplier-difference modulus tends uniformly to $2$.

By [F3], the squared relative $L^2$ error is the average of $|e^{i\Delta_n}-1|^2$ over $\Xi_n$ with respect to normalized Lebesgue measure. Since step 3.1 gives uniform convergence of that modulus to $2$, the averages of its square tend to $4$; the relative errors are nonnegative, so they tend to $2$, not $0$. This contradicts the Statement refuted and proves the claimed counterexample.

historical_source_interface.exact_statement:
Fix a named positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$, spatial domain $\mathbb R^3$, and time domain $\mathbb R$. Adopt SI
units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $z\in\mathbb R$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive on $D_\delta$, and define the exact scalar
and paraxial scalar propagators as the $L^2$ equivalence classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[ e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)}\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=e^{ik_0z}\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[ e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
A candidate monochromatic vector plane-wave mode at frequency $\omega$ has
complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ in the real-field
encoding $e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot(x,y,z)-\omega t)}$. It is called an exact
source-free vacuum mode only when its associated real fields satisfy the
adopted source-free vacuum Maxwell equations. The longitudinal electric
coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

Let $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, and $s\in[0,\delta^2]$. Define

$$R(s):=1-\frac{s}{2}-\sqrt{1-s}.$$

Then

$$R(s)=\frac{s^2}{4\left(1-\frac{s}{2}+\sqrt{1-s}\right)},\qquad 0\le R(s)\le\frac{s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},$$

and

$$\left|e^{izk_0\sqrt{1-s}}-e^{izk_0(1-s/2)}\right| \le \frac{|z|k_0s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}.$$

More generally, for all real $a,b$,
$$|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

risk_review.notes: Read all five steps and direct box-measure, exponential, modulus, Plancherel and local bound suppliers. For n>=1, delta_n<=1/3, the rectangle side lengths R_n delta_n/8 are positive and its upper squared normalized radius is 1-delta_n/4+delta_n^2/32<=1. Thus its normalized indicator is a nonzero L2 input with fixed norm A_star under Countable Choice. The lower normalized radius tends uniformly to one on these varying sets; the remainder denominator tends uniformly to 2 and stays positive. Substitution of z_n=8pi/(k0 delta_n^4) gives Delta_n->pi uniformly. Modulus multiplicativity handles the negative actual phase, and reverse triangle plus the phase Lipschitz estimate gives uniform modulus convergence to 2. Averages of squares on the normalized positive-measure rectangles therefore tend to 4 without any unjustified exchange of a varying-domain limit and integral; nonnegative roots give error 2. This refutes precisely the universal convergence claim, with no conclusion for fixed distance or arbitrary aperture outputs. No defect.

citations.quote:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and

and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable

and define the paraxial multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}.$$
The exact scalar and paraxial scalar propagators are the $L^2$ equivalence

$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$

and $\mathbf b$ has units tesla. The candidate is an **exact

jointly $C^1$ and satisfy, pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$,
$$\operatorname{div}\mathbf E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf B=c^{-2}\partial_t\mathbf E,$$
the zero-source specialization of the adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell branch.
The longitudinal electric coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we relabel the function values at $0,1,2$ by $1,2,3$ and write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. $$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), which is what makes the encoded expressions differentiable in the plane-wave form; derivations that differentiate them use [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and the chain rule for holomorphic maps where they are applied.

Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. No electromagnetic interpretation, equation of motion or physical identification is part of this definition.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is

([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:

equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Since $\kappa\le\delta k_0<k_0$, $k_z=\sqrt{k_0^2-\kappa^2}$ is positive. The definitions give $\kappa^2+k_z^2=k_0^2$, $\kappa E_0+k_ze_z=0$, and $\omega b_y=k_0^2E_0/k_z$. Thus $\mathbf K=(\kappa,0,k_z)$ is a forward wavevector of length $k_0$, and $\mathbf e$ is transverse to it.

By [F3], for each spatial coordinate $x_j$, $\partial_{x_j}E=\operatorname{Re}(iK_je\,e^{i\phi})$ componentwise, and $\partial_tE=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega e\,e^{i\phi})$; the same formulas hold with $B,b$ in place of $E,e$. From [step 1.1], $$\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf e=\kappa E_0+k_ze_z=0,\qquad \mathbf K\cdot\mathbf b=0,$$ $$\mathbf K\times\mathbf e= \left(0,k_zE_0-\kappa e_z,0\right) =\left(0,\frac{k_0^2E_0}{k_z},0\right)=\omega\mathbf b,$$ and $$\mathbf K\times\mathbf b= \left(-k_zb_y,0,\kappa b_y\right) =\left(-\frac{k_0^2E_0}{\omega},0, \frac{\kappa k_0^2E_0}{\omega k_z}\right) =-\frac{\omega}{c^2}\mathbf e,$$ where the last equality uses $k_0=\omega/c$. Summing the spatial derivatives therefore yields $$\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{Re}(i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf e)e^{i\phi})=0, \qquad \operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{Re}(i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf b)e^{i\phi})=0,$$ $$\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}(i(\mathbf K\times\mathbf e)e^{i\phi}) =-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\operatorname{Re}(i(\mathbf K\times\mathbf b)e^{i\phi}) =c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$ Thus all four source-free Maxwell equations in [A1] hold pointwise, so these real fields are an exact mode.

The constructed transverse amplitude is $(E_0,0)$. Applying [F4] gives $e_z=-\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf e_\perp/k_z=-\kappa E_0/k_z$ and $|e_z|/|E_0|\le\delta/\sqrt{1-\delta^2}$. Since $\kappa>0$, $E_0\ne0$, and $k_z>0$, $e_z\ne0$. Hence the alternative $e_z=0$ with this same transverse amplitude is incompatible with source-free Maxwell transversality.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a named positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$, spatial domain $\mathbb R^3$, and time domain $\mathbb R$. Adopt SI
units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive there. For each $z\in\mathbb R$, define the
exact multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=\begin{cases}e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)},&\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta,\\0,&\boldsymbol\xi\notin D_\delta,\end{cases}$$
and define the paraxial multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}.$$
The exact scalar and paraxial scalar propagators are the $L^2$ equivalence
classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
For complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ at frequency
$\omega$, the real-field encoding assigns the maps
$\mathbf E,\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by
$$\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf e e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right),\qquad \mathbf B(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf b e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right).$$
In the SI field interpretation, $\mathbf e$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$
and $\mathbf b$ has units tesla. The candidate is an **exact
source-free vacuum plane-wave mode** precisely when these real fields are
jointly $C^1$ and satisfy, pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$,
$$\operatorname{div}\mathbf E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf B=c^{-2}\partial_t\mathbf E,$$
the zero-source specialization of the adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell branch.
The longitudinal electric coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, a parameter $\omega>0$ and amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we relabel the function values at $0,1,2$ by $1,2,3$ and write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. For $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], the real number $\sum_{j=1}^3k_jx_j$; for $t\in\mathbb R$ put

$$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), which is what makes the encoded expressions differentiable in the plane-wave form; derivations that differentiate them use [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and the chain rule for holomorphic maps where they are applied.

Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. No electromagnetic interpretation, equation of motion or physical identification is part of this definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. For $n\ge1$, these are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of The derivative and the Riemann integral of a vector-valued function: an intrinsic derivative and a componentwise integral.

For $n=0$, use the zero-space case directly, without invoking that supplier's positive-codomain standing hypothesis. The space $\mathbb R^0$ has only its zero vector and carries the zero Euclidean norm and its induced metric (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5, The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms). Whenever the line map is defined near $0$, every difference quotient for real $t\ne0$ is this zero vector; define $D_vf(a)=0$. This is the unique possible derivative value, and its normwise difference-quotient error is exactly zero for all such $t$, so the real parameter still approaches an actual limit point. Every existing coordinate direction therefore has $\partial_jf(a)=0$; these zero-valued partial maps are continuous in the induced norm metrics. If the source dimension is zero, there are no partial indices and the sole direction is $v=0$; its constant line map is defined near $0$.
